summary: Tuktoyaktuk / James Gruben Airport (YUB) serves the small Inuvialuit hamlet of Tuktoyaktuk, located on the Arctic Ocean at the mouth of the Mackenzie River in Canada's Northwest Territories. The airport is named in honor of James Gruben, a respected community leader. It functions as a vital lifeline for this remote northern community, supporting passenger travel, medevac services, and cargo to one of Canada's most northerly road-accessible settlements.
faqs:
Q: What is Tuktoyaktuk Airport primarily used for?
A: It primarily serves the local Inuvialuit community with passenger flights, mail delivery, medical evacuations, and freight, connecting to Inuvik and other northern hubs.

Q: When is the airport open?
A: As a small northern airport, operations are typically limited to daylight hours and may be affected by weather, especially in winter.

Q: Are there scheduled commercial flights to YUB?
A: Service is limited and not year-round; flights are generally provided by small regional carriers such as Aklak Air, depending on demand and season.

Q: What is the nearest larger airport?
A: Inuvik (Mike Zubko) Airport, approximately 130 km south, is the closest airport with more frequent service.
transport_tips: Since 2017, Tuktoyaktuk has been accessible year-round by road via the Inuvik-Tuktoyaktuk Highway, but most visitors without a vehicle still arrive by air. Ground transportation from the airport is very limited, so arranging a pickup or rental in advance is strongly recommended. There are no taxi stands or rideshare services; many visitors pre-arrange transport with local accommodations or guides.
local_tip: If visiting in late summer, ask locals about the pingos nearby — Tuktoyaktuk has some of the largest ice-cored hills in the world, and they are a short ride from the airport and a highlight most travelers never expect.
